When I first heard about the Searchlight Institute, [I can't
say](https://www.rollingstone.com/politics/political-commentary/democrats-
searchlight-institute-think-tank-polling-housing-1235432471/) I loved the
premise. Did Washington _really_ need one more centrist think tank that's
skeptical about progressive policy ideas?

After I snarkily criticized one of their polls on Twitter, their team reached
out to me, offering **Zeteo** an opportunity to help them write a lengthy poll
exclusively about Medicare for All. Of course I said yes: I strongly believe
in the project of universal healthcare, something that is standard virtually
everywhere else in the world.

Searchlight may favor [more limited
ways](https://www.nbcnews.com/politics/politics-news/democrats-free-primary-
care-all-healthcare-elections-rcna345145) to expand healthcare access, but no
other DC think tank had ever offered me a chance to partner on a poll before
about Medicare for All - and definitely not for free. According to
[Searchlight](https://www.searchlightinstitute.org/wp-
content/uploads/2026/07/Memo_-An-Honest-Assessment-of-Voter-Attitudes-Toward-
Government-Run-Health-Insurance.pdf), we collaborated on "a first-of-its-kind
honest assessment of voter attitudes on government-run health insurance."

Our joint [survey](https://www.searchlightinstitute.org/wp-
content/uploads/2026/07/EMBARGOED-Zeteo-x-Searchlight-Health-Care-Wording-
Test-Survey-1.pdf), conducted by Tavern Research,
[found](https://www.searchlightinstitute.org/wp-
content/uploads/2026/07/Crosstabs-Searchlight-June-
Omni-20260624_110103-1-1.pdf) single-payer proposals received either majority
or plurality support, depending on how they were worded. The poll found strong
support for the idea of having the government cover a variety of healthcare
costs. It also found widespread skepticism about the government's ability to
run a national healthcare program, even though many Americans already get
health insurance through the government.

In terms of the single-payer questions presented, the version that polled best
was when people were asked, simply, if they support automatically enrolling
every American in a comprehensive government-administered health insurance
plan, something like the Medicare coverage that people 65 and older get.
